column2: Someone multiplied two matrices, A and B, and handed you the answer, C. Is C really A times B? You could multiply them again.
Nine entries, three multiplications each, twenty-seven in all. With a thousand rows and columns, a billion.
Checking one entry at random is cheap, but it misses a single wrong entry eight times in nine.
Here is a better check. Toss a coin for each column of C, and add up the columns that land heads.
Do the same to B, then multiply by A. That takes nine multiplications, not twenty-seven.
Both columns must match if C is right. They don't, so C is wrong, for certain.
But that was one toss. Of the eight ways three coins can land, how many miss the wrong entry?
Check all eight. Four of them miss, exactly half.
Because every miss leaves out the column that holds the wrong entry.
But no wrong answer hides from more than half the tosses. So toss again. Twenty fresh tosses all miss less than once in a million.
